title: Nifty 50 Profits Seen Growing 20% as Earnings Accelerate Despite Market Slump
excerpt: Five brokerages expect Nifty 50 net profit to rise about 20% in the September quarter, building on a 10-quarter high — even as record foreign selling pushes the index toward its worst year in 15.
body:
• Nifty 50 companies are forecast to post average net profit growth of about 20% year-on-year for the September quarter, up from a 10-quarter high of 18% in the June quarter, according to estimates from five brokerages compiled by Reuters.
  • Motilal Oswal is the most bullish at 27% — the fastest in 17 quarters — while PhillipCapital sees a modest 13%, reflecting margin pressure outside oil and gas.
  • Banks are expected to be the earnings anchor, with healthy loan growth, lower credit costs and fewer bad loans; automobiles and new-age tech platforms are the other favoured sectors.
  • For investors: the profit rebound is the counterweight to a grim stock market — foreign investors have sold Indian equities at a record pace, pushing the Nifty toward its worst year in 15. Earnings, not flows, will decide whether the recovery holds.

Indian companies are expected to accelerate their profit growth in the September quarter even as foreign investors flee the country's stocks and global headwinds pile up, according to brokerage estimates compiled by Reuters — a divergence that will test whether earnings can finally pull the market out of its slump.

Nifty 50 firms' net profit is forecast to rise about 20% year-on-year on average, based on estimates from five brokerages. That would build on the June quarter's 18%, itself a 10-quarter high that followed three quarters of low-single-digit growth. Tata Consultancy Services was due to kick off the earnings season later on Thursday — its results have already been reported separately.

Banks carry the load

"JPMorgan analysts led by Rajiv Batra pointed to "resilient domestic demand in Q2, early festive inventory build-up" and favourable pricing in commodity-linked sectors as the supports for earnings."

Most analysts back financials as the principal earnings anchor: healthy loan growth, lower credit costs and fewer loans turning bad at banks. Motilal Oswal, the most optimistic of the five at a 27% profit-growth forecast — the fastest in 17 quarters — is bullish on automobiles and new-age tech platforms, naming Meesho, PhysicsWallah, Mahindra & Mahindra and TVS Motor as picks on structural growth trends, recovering discretionary demand and expanding product portfolios. JPMorgan analysts led by Rajiv Batra pointed to "resilient domestic demand in Q2, early festive inventory build-up" and favourable pricing in commodity-linked sectors as the supports for earnings.

The outlier is PhillipCapital, which expects a modest 13% rise, reflecting margin pressure and a less favourable earnings mix outside the oil and gas sector. The spread between 13% and 27% captures the core debate: is this a broad-based corporate recovery or one concentrated in banks and commodity-linked giants?

The headwinds are real

The optimism sits against an ugly market backdrop. Foreign investors have pulled out of Indian stocks at a record pace, pushing the Nifty 50 toward its worst year in 15 years. The weakest monsoon in a decade has raised concerns about rural demand just as the festive season approaches, and the escalating Middle East conflict has fuelled global inflation worries, raising the risk premium on emerging-market equities.

The June-quarter numbers offer some comfort. Bank of Baroda Research found aggregate net profit of listed companies (excluding banks, financials and oil firms) rose 23.7% in the fiscal first quarter, with net sales up 17.5% — driven partly by a low base, rupee depreciation and firm commodity prices, but also by the consumption stimulus from last year's GST cuts.

What it means for investors

For the diaspora investor with exposure to India — through mutual funds, ETFs or direct holdings — the message is that corporate fundamentals and market prices are telling different stories. Record foreign selling has decoupled the Nifty from the earnings trajectory; if the 20% profit growth materialises, valuations become harder to argue against. But the risks flagged by the bearish camp are the ones that break forecasts: a poor monsoon hitting rural consumption, and oil prices spiking on Middle East escalation, which would squeeze margins across the board.

What to watch

The next two weeks decide the narrative. Bank earnings will show whether credit growth is holding up; automakers' festive-season wholesale numbers will test the rural-demand story; and management commentary on margins — especially from consumer and industrial companies — will reveal whether PhillipCapital's caution or Motilal Oswal's exuberance was closer to the mark. Also on the calendar: whether foreign selling pauses, because earnings upgrades mean little if the flows keep draining.
